          ⚙ Compiler flags for stack analysis
          
        

        

          

            Add these flags to your project. In S32DS: Project → Properties → C/C++ Build → Settings → Compiler → Miscellaneous → Other flags
          

          

            -fstack-usage
            Generates .su files — per-function stack frame size and type (static/dynamic). Required for Level 1 analysis.
          

          

            -fcallgraph-info=su,da
            Generates .ci call-graph files in VCG format — enables worst-case call chain and DFS stack depth. Required for Level 2 analysis.
          

          

            -g3
            Full DWARF debug info — enables source line interleaving in disassembly, precise addr2line, and crash source resolution. Minimal code-size impact when optimising.
          

          

            -Wstack-usage=256
            Build-time warning when any function frame exceeds 256 bytes. Tune the value to match your RTOS task stack size.
          

          

            -fno-inline-small-functions
            Prevents the compiler from inlining small functions, making stack analysis more accurate (inlined functions don't appear in .su files).
          

          

            -fno-omit-frame-pointer
            Keeps the frame pointer register (r7 on Cortex-M). Improves debuggability; allows stack unwinding from crash handlers even without DWARF.
          

          

            💡 All flags can coexist with any optimisation level (-O0, -O1, -Os, -O2). 
            Start with -fstack-usage -fcallgraph-info=su,da -g3 -Wstack-usage=256.

⚠ Hazard detail
            
            

              
            

          

          

        


        
        

          
📚 ISR stack budget explained

          

            

              

                Why ISR stack is larger than .su reports

                The compiler's -fstack-usage output only shows what
                your code's prologue pushes. Before your first instruction runs,
                the CPU (ARM Cortex-M) or OS (Linux) has already pushed a context frame.
                On Cortex-M this is 8 registers × 4 bytes = 32 bytes; with FPU lazy
                stacking up to 72 additional bytes can be saved. Add this overhead
                to every ISR's frame budget.
              

              

                Why nested interrupts multiply consumption

                If your system allows interrupt nesting (ARM: PRIMASK=0 / configurable
                NVIC priority), a high-priority IRQ can preempt a running ISR.
                At worst, every enabled ISR's full stack budget is simultaneously
                consumed. Your task stack needs room for the deepest nesting chain.
                Total = Σ(task_frame) + Σ(concurrent_ISR_budgets).
              

              

                Fast memory requirement

                ISR latency = interrupt latency + ISR instruction fetch time.
                If ISR code sits in flash (slow), every fetch takes 3–8× longer
                than SRAM/TCAM. On ESP32, ISRs must be decorated with
                IRAM_ATTR. On STM32/S32K, place ISRs in ITCM via
                __attribute__((section(".itcm_code"))).
              

              

                Processing time estimate

                "Est. cycles" = (code_size ÷ avg_bytes_per_insn) × avg_CPI.
                This is a rough order-of-magnitude only — compilers mix instruction
                sizes, pipelines vary, and cache effects dominate. Use it to
                compare ISRs relative to each other, not as an absolute timing.
                For accurate measurement, use a logic analyser or DWT cycle counter.

🗂 Vtables & RTTI polymorphic classes from _ZTV* / _ZTI* symbols

          

            What is a vtable?
            Every class with a virtual function gets a vtable — a read-only array of function pointers.
            Each object has a hidden vptr (first 8 or 4 bytes) → vtable → function.
            Virtual dispatch = 3 memory accesses vs 1 for non-virtual.
            Native vs cross-compiled: on x86-64 Linux vtables live in .data.rel.ro (relocated by ld.so);
            on ARM/ESP32 they live in .rodata in flash (absolute addresses, no relocation needed).
          

          

            Class nameVtable symbolSizeVirtual slotsRTTI
          

        

        

          
📐 Template instantiations grouped by template family · click row to expand

          

            Template code bloat:
            Each distinct argument set compiles to a separate copy of the code.
            Reduce with explicit instantiation (template class std::vector<int>;), type erasure, or policy classes.

⚡ Exception handling .eh_frame · .gcc_except_table · .ARM.exidx

          

            Exception tables exist even without try/catch.
            GCC emits .eh_frame CFI for every function unless you pass -fno-exceptions -fno-unwind-tables.
            On ARM: .ARM.exidx + .ARM.extab (compact 4-byte-per-function format).
            On x86-64 native: removing .eh_frame breaks GDB, perf, and glibc backtrace() — don't remove it.
          

          
SectionSizePurpose

          

        

        

          
🔗 Dynamic linking — PLT / GOT native Linux only — absent in cross-compiled firmware

          

        

        

          
🔨 Global constructor / destructor order .init_array · .fini_array — run before/after main()

          

            

              Static initialisation order fiasco:
              Constructors of globals in different translation units run in link order (undefined across TUs).
              If global A's constructor reads global B and B hasn't been constructed yet, you get undefined behaviour.
              Fix: use Meyers singleton (static Type& get()) to enforce lazy initialisation order.
